title: Why Over-Tightening Plastic Threaded Fittings Causes Leaks
description: When joining threaded plastic fittings, applying extra torque does not guarantee a better seal. Standard National Pipe Taper (NPT) threads are tapered, meaning the diameter increases as the pipe enters the fitting. As you thread a male adapter into a female plastic socket, the tapered design acts as a wedge, placing constant outward stress on the plastic collar. Over-tightening stretches the material beyond its tensile limit, creating hairline stress cracks that often fail hours or days later. For plastic threaded joints, hand-tighten the fitting first, then turn it only 1 to 2 times with a wrench to secure the seal.

visual_story: The viewer immediately notices a close-up view of a threaded PVC connection with a visible hairline split along the female adapter collar. The visual highlights the physical consequence of mechanical over-torquing on tapered threads. It proves to the viewer that plastic fittings do not simply deform under high torque—they experience structural expansion failure, demonstrating why mechanical moderation is required during assembly.

on_image_text.hook: Over-tightening plastic fittings creates hidden cracks.
on_image_text.explanation: Tapered threads act like a wedge, creating constant outward tension against female plastic sockets.
on_image_text.takeaway: Hand-tighten plastic threaded joints, then add only 1 to 2 turns with a wrench.
